How Many Numbers Does a Face Need?

A 60 × 50 face is 3000 numbers. Project it onto the top k eigenfaces and it becomes k numbers; multiply them back by the eigenfaces and add the average face, and you get an approximation of the original. Slide k from 0 to 336 and watch what each extra number buys, for faces and for a palm tree.

What to compress

Every image is normalized the way the notebook normalizes the faces: its 3000 values minus their mean, divided by their standard deviation.

Numbers kept per face

Shows a tiny image with about k pixels next to the reconstruction, blown back up to 60 × 50.

Readout

Numbers stored per image. The average face and the k eigenfaces are stored once and shared by every face.

the notebook's projection and reconstruction 

    


  






  

    
Why 336 and not 3000
337 faces, once the average is subtracted, span at most 336 directions of the 3000-dimensional pixel space. Along every other direction the faces do not vary at all, so only 336 eigenvalues are non-zero, and 336 eigenfaces are enough to rebuild any of the 337 faces exactly.

    
Variance kept is an average
The blue curve is one curve for the whole dataset: the share of all the faces' variation that the top k eigenfaces hold. The orange curve is for one image. Summed over all 337 faces, the squared lengths of what is lost make up exactly the share the blue curve does not keep, the gap above it. A single face can be easier or harder than that average, and the palm tree is much harder: at k = 10 it keeps an error of 0.91, while the ten faces in the list range from 0.37 to 0.78.

    
The face space
The eigenfaces span a "face space" inside the space of all 60 × 50 images. Reconstruction finds the closest point in that space. A training face lies inside it; a palm tree does not, and the part of the tree that sticks out of face space can never be rebuilt, however many eigenfaces you use.
